what: Brookfield Business Corporation owns controlling stakes in operating businesses. It is the corporate share class of Brookfield’s private equity arm, and its holdings have included industrial manufacturing, road fuel distribution, nuclear engineering services, modular building leasing and healthcare operations — bought, improved and eventually sold.
customers: It has no customers itself. Its subsidiaries serve their own markets, from motorists at service stations to utilities needing nuclear plant services, and its shareholders are investors wanting exposure to Brookfield’s private equity results in a listed form.
money: The combined revenue of the operating businesses it controls, which changes substantially as businesses are bought and sold.
moat: The advantage is Brookfield’s access to deals and its willingness to buy complicated, capital-intensive businesses that other buyers avoid — often from distressed sellers. It holds for long periods, improves operations and sells at a higher multiple. Consolidating the subsidiaries means the accounts show the businesses themselves rather than an investment value.
risks: Debt of $38.9B against $3.2B of cash looks alarming until you understand it sits at the subsidiaries rather than at the parent, but it is still real leverage against real businesses.
Reported net income of $22.0M on $27.0B of revenue, and a price/earnings ratio of 259, make the earnings line meaningless as a valuation input.
Revenue fell from $57.4B in 2022 to $27.5B in 2025 because businesses were sold, so revenue tells you about portfolio changes rather than performance.
Free cash flow of about negative $911.0M reflects acquisitions and subsidiary capital spending rather than operating losses.
The value depends on asset sales happening at good prices, and that depends on markets being willing to buy.
opportunities: EV/EBITDA of 7.3 on the consolidated businesses is a reasonable price for a collection of industrial and service operations.
Brookfield has a long record of buying complicated assets cheaply and selling them higher, which is the entire proposition.
The holdings are deliberately unglamorous and capital-intensive, which is where competition for assets is lowest.
Eight analysts average a $37.69 target against a $27.85 price, about 35% above.
watch: Realisations: what gets sold and at what multiple versus what was paid. Every other number here is an accounting artefact of consolidation.
view: Brookfield Business Corporation is an accounting puzzle wrapped around a straightforward idea. The idea is Brookfield’s private equity business: buy complicated, capital-heavy, unfashionable companies — often from sellers who need to sell — improve how they run, and sell them later at a higher multiple. The puzzle is that because the stakes are controlling, the accounts consolidate the subsidiaries, so you see $27 billion of revenue, $22 million of net income, $38.9 billion of debt and a price/earnings ratio of 259. None of those figures mean what they appear to.

The debt is the one that frightens people most and is the most frequently misread. It sits at the operating subsidiaries, each financed on its own assets, not at the parent — so a failure at one business does not cascade. That is a genuine structural protection and it is how private equity has always worked. But it is still leverage against real cash flows, and the model depends on each business carrying its own borrowing comfortably.

The revenue decline from $57 billion to $27.5 billion looks like collapse and is mostly the opposite: businesses were sold, which is the point of the model. This is the single most important thing to understand here. Revenue going down can be good news, revenue going up can be a sign of expensive acquisitions, and neither tells you anything about whether value was created. Only realisations do — what got sold, for what multiple, against what was paid.

Which is also the limitation. You are buying a manager’s judgement, visible only in hindsight, in a vehicle whose financial statements actively obscure it. At 7.3 times EV/EBITDA the consolidated businesses are not expensively priced, and Brookfield’s record is good. But the honest statement is that this requires trusting the manager rather than analysing the company, and that an investor who cannot assess realisation history over a full cycle is not really analysing anything at all.
bull: Brookfield keeps buying complicated assets cheaply and realising them at higher multiples, with subsidiary-level debt insulating each holding and 7.3 times EV/EBITDA understating the portfolio.
bear: Exit markets close, highly leveraged subsidiaries struggle to refinance, and consolidated accounts hide deterioration until a realisation comes in below cost.
